questions.knowledge_point: Reconstructing a Two-Variable Function From Its Gradient
questions.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y)=F(x,y),$ the function $f(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=3-x
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (-y)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-xy+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-x+{g}^{′}(y).
$$

Taking  $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=3-x$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-x+{g}^{′}(y) & =3-x \\ {g}^{′}(y) & =3 \\ g(y) & =3y+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)=3y+C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y)=-xy+3y+C.
$$

The gradient of the function $f(x,y)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y)=F(x,y),$ the function $f(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}={e}^{y}-y\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{y}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int ({e}^{y}-y\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{e}^{y}+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{y}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{g}^{′}(y).
$$

Taking  $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{y}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x{e}^{y}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{g}^{′}(y) & =x{e}^{y}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {g}^{′}(y) & =0 \\ g(y) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)=C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C.
$$

The gradient of the function $f(x,y)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y)=F(x,y),$ the function $f(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x{y}^{2}+1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}y+1
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (2x{y}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}{y}^{2}+x+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}y+{g}^{′}(y).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}y+1$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}y+{g}^{′}(y) & =2{x}^{2}y+1 \\ {g}^{′}(y) & =1 \\ g(y) & =y+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)=y+C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}+x+y+C.
$$

The gradient of the function $f(x,y)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j.

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)+y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)+x
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)+y)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)+xy+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)+x+{g}^{′}(y).
$$

Taking  $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)+x$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)+x+{g}^{′}(y) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)+x \\ {g}^{′}(y) & =0 \\ g(y) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)=C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)+xy+C.
$$

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y)=F(x,y),$ the function $f(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡y
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+{g}^{′}(y).
$$

Taking  $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+{g}^{′}(y) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡y \\ {g}^{′}(y) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡y \\ g(y) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡y+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡y+C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y-\operatorname{cos}⁡y+C.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Reconstructing a Three-Variable Function From Its Gradient
questions.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,k.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2xz+\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}={x}^{2}
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (2xz+\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}z+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int 0\,\text{d}y \\  & =h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}z+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}={x}^{2}+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}={x}^{2}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+{h}^{′}(z) \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ h(z) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}z+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+C.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Reconstructing a Three-Variable Function From Its Gradient
questions.problem:
Consider the function

$$
F(x,y,z)=(yz{e}^{xz}+z)\,i+({e}^{xz}+1)\,j+(xy{e}^{xz}+x)\,k.
$$

Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z).$
questions.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{i}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,\text{j}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,\text{k}.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=yz{e}^{xz}+z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{xz}+1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=xy{e}^{xz}+x
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (yz{e}^{xz}+z)\,\text{d}x \\  & =y{e}^{xz}+xz+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{xz}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{xz}+1$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{xz}+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & ={e}^{xz}+1 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int 1\,\text{d}y \\  & =y+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=y+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=y{e}^{xz}+xz+y+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}=xy{e}^{xz}+x+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=xy{e}^{xz}+x$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}xy{e}^{xz}+x+{h}^{′}(z) & =zy{e}^{xz}+x \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ h(z) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=y{e}^{xz}+xz+y+C.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Reconstructing a Three-Variable Function From Its Gradient
questions.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,k.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{ln}⁡y+1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{y}-{z}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-2yz
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\operatorname{ln}⁡y+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+x+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{y}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{y}-{z}^{2}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{y}+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{x}{y}-{z}^{2} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =-{z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int (-{z}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =-y{z}^{2}+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=-y{z}^{2}+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+x-y{z}^{2}+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-2yz+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-2yz$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-2yz & =-2yz+{h}^{′}(z) \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ h(z) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+x-y{z}^{2}+C.
$$

The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,k.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y{z}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{z}^{2}+z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=2xyz+y-2
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int y{z}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =xy{z}^{2}+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{z}^{2}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{z}^{2}+z$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x{z}^{2}+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =x{z}^{2}+z \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =z\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int z\,\text{d}y \\  & =yz+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=yz+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=xy{z}^{2}+yz+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}=2xyz+y+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=2xyz+y-2$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2xyz+y-2 & =2xyz+y+{h}^{′}(z) \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =-2 \\ h(z) & =-2z+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=xy{z}^{2}+yz-2z+C.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find $f(x,y)$ such that $\nabla f = \mathbf{F},$ where $\mathbf F(x,y) = 2xy\ \mathbf i + (x^2 - 3)\ \mathbf j .$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y)$ is defined as

$$
\nabla f(x,y) = \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}}\,\textbf{i} + \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}}\,\textbf{j}.
$$

Since $\nabla f(x,y) = \mathbf F(x,y),$ the function $f(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}} = 2xy, \qquad \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} = x^2-3.
$$

First, we integrate $\dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int 2xy\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}y+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} = x^2 + g'(y).
$$

Taking $\dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} = x^2 -3$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{g}^{′}(y) & ={x}^{2}-3 \\ {g}^{′}(y) & =-3 \\ g(y) & =-3y+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)=-3y +C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y) = x^2y -3y + C.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $\nabla f(x,y,z)  = \mathbf{F}(x,y,z),$ where $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = yz\,\mathbf{i} + (xz + 4z^2)\,\mathbf{j} + (xy+8yz)\,\mathbf{k}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
\nabla f(x,y,z) = \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}} \, \mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} \, \mathbf{j} + \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{z}} \, \mathbf{k}.
$$

Since $\nabla f(x,y,z)  = \mathbf{F}(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}} = yz, \qquad \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} = xz + 4z^2, \qquad \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{z}} = xy+8yz.
$$

First, we integrate $\dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int yz\,\text{d}x \\  & =xyz+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} = xz + \dfrac{\partial{g}}{\partial{y}}.
$$

Taking $\dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} = xz + 4z^2$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}xz+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =xz+4{z}^{2} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =4{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\dfrac{\partial{g}}{\partial{y}}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int 4{z}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =4y{z}^{2}+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z) = 4yz^2 + h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x, y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z) = xyz + 4yz^2 + h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{z}} = xy + 8yz + h'(z).
$$

Taking $\dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{z}} = xy+8yz$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}xy+8yz & =xy+8yz+{h}^{′}(z) \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ h(z) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z) = xyz + 4yz^2 + C.
$$
